# Overview

Analyzing questions related to OSPO activities and services.

Research questions:\
- What services do OSPOs most commonly offer?\
- How do OSPOs spend the bulk of their time?\
- Do differently-located OSPOs offer different services?

Survey questions:\
- Tick the activities your OSPO actually carries out today:\
  - Developing and sharing best practices (best_practices)\
  - Educational efforts (edu_efforts)\
  - External partnerships and tech transfer (ext_partnerships)\
  - [Supporting tools and infrastructure (tools_infra) - not analyzed here, see tools notebook]\
  - Community building (comm_building)\
  - Directly supporting open source projects (project_support)\
  - Advocacy and policy (advocacy_policy)\
  - Funding and financial support (funding_support)\
  - OSPO operations (ospo_ops)\
- Of the activities above, which take the most of your own time? Rank your top three. (ranking)\

## Do differently-located OSPOs offer different services? (one response per ospo)

To begin, let's create a data frame with each organization and its various locations.

```{r}
ospo_loc$organization <- org_responses$organization
loc <- consolidate_org_responses_yn(ospo_loc)
```


```{r}
# Use tibble::lst() so object names are kept as category names
df_list <- lst(bp_consolidated, edu_consolidated, ext_consolidated, tools_consolidated, cb_consolidated, ps_consolidated, ap_consolidated, fs_consolidated, ospo_consolidated)

# Classify organizations (accounting for `joint` and all-"No" rows)
other_cols <- setdiff(names(loc), c("organization", "tto"))
org_groups <- loc |>
  mutate(
    total_yes = rowSums(across(-organization, ~ .x == "Yes"), na.rm = TRUE),
    group = case_when(
      library == "Yes" & total_yes == 1 ~ "Library_only",
      tto == "Yes"     & total_yes == 1 ~ "TTO_only",
      total_yes >= 1                    ~ "Other",
      TRUE                              ~ NA_character_
    ),
    group = factor(group, levels = c("Library_only", "TTO_only", "Other"))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(group)) |>
  select(organization, group)

# Keep commented for privacy
# head(org_groups)
# Check group sample sizes
# count(org_groups, group)
```

Calculate engagement in the nine "super-categories" by group

```{r}
# Calculate % with at least one "Yes" per group
calc_yes_pct <- function(df, df_name, group_lookup) {
  df %>%
    inner_join(group_lookup, by = "organization") %>%
    mutate(
      # TRUE if any column (besides organization and group) equals "Yes"
      any_yes = if_any(-c(organization, group), ~ .x == "Yes")
    ) %>%
    group_by(group) %>%
    summarise(
      n_orgs = n(),
      n_yes = sum(any_yes, na.rm = TRUE),
      pct_yes = mean(any_yes, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(dataset = df_name, .before = 1)
}

# Run function across all data frames and combine into one summary table
results <- imap(df_list, ~ calc_yes_pct(.x, .y, org_groups)) %>%
  list_rbind()

results
```

```{r}
services_long <- df_list |>
  lapply(\(df) {
    pivot_longer(
      df,
      cols = -organization,
      names_to = "service",
      values_to = "offered"
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "category") |>
  mutate(
    category = sub("_consolidated$", "", category),
    offered  = factor(offered, levels = c("Yes", "No"))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(offered))

# Keep commented for privacy!
# head(services_long)
```

```{r}
service_comparison <- services_long |>
  inner_join(org_groups, by = "organization") |>
  group_by(category, service) |>
  summarise(
    pct_tto = round(100 * mean(offered[group == "TTO_only"] == "Yes"), 1),
    pct_lib = round(100 * mean(offered[group == "Library_only"] == "Yes"), 1),
    pct_oth = round(100 * mean(offered[group == "Other"] == "Yes"), 1),
    p_val   = fisher.test(table(group, offered))$p.value,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    max_spread = pmax(pct_lib, pct_tto, pct_oth) - pmin(pct_lib, pct_tto, pct_oth),
    p_adj      = p.adjust(p_val, method = "BH")
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(max_spread))

subset(service_comparison, p_val < 0.05)
```

Technically none of these are statistically significant by the Fisher's exact test, but I think they are all socially significant.

Let's export all rows, and the most interesting columns, to a tsv.

```{r}
# Filter codebook to these sata questions only (others will have NA in tip column)
service_lookup <- codebook |>
  filter(!is.na(tip)) |>
  distinct(nickname, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(nickname, service_full = tip)

category_labels <- c(
  bp    = "Developing and sharing best practices",
  edu   = "Educational efforts",
  ext   = "External partnerships and tech transfer",
  tools = "Supporting tools and infrastructure",
  cb    = "Community building",
  ps    = "Directly supporting open source projects",
  ap    = "Advocacy and policy",
  fs    = "Funding and financial support",
  ospo  = "OSPO operations and strategy"
)

# Join full service text and replace category codes
service_comparison_clean <- service_comparison |>
  left_join(service_lookup, by = c("service" = "nickname")) |>
  mutate(
    # coalesce() keeps the original nickname if a match isn't found
    service  = coalesce(service_full, service),
    category = recode(category, !!!category_labels)
  ) |>
  select(-service_full)
```

```{r}
service_comparison_clean <- service_comparison_clean |>
  select(-p_val, -max_spread) |>
  arrange(p_adj)

write_df_to_file(service_comparison_clean, "service_comparison.tsv")
```

## Quantifying "commonness" or "pervasiveness"

I'd love to get a single number that represents how common or widespread each activity category is. Because the subcategories each have their own score, I'm not sure that there's a clear-cut way to do this. So here I'm trying a couple of different things and trying to decide what is most intuitive and accurate.

First, let's take the average score of all the subcategories in each category.
```{r}
how_common <- sapply(df_list, function(df) mean(df$count, na.rm = TRUE))
names(how_common) <- c("bp", "edu", "ext", "tools", "cb", "ps", "ap", "fs", "ospo")
how_common <- sort(how_common, decreasing = TRUE)
how_common
```

Next, let's try taking the maximum, most widespread sub-category/sub-activity. How does this change the order of the ranking?
```{r}
how_common <- sapply(df_list, function(df) max(df$count, na.rm = TRUE))
names(how_common) <- c("bp", "edu", "ext", "tools", "cb", "ps", "ap", "fs", "ospo")
how_common <- sort(how_common, decreasing = TRUE)
how_common
```

Wow, that does change the ranking quite a bit. We need a different approach.

Okay, starting over. I want a simple metric so I'm not going to consolidate by organization. I'm just going to ask, how many people checked at least one activity in this category, for each category.
```{r}
best_practices <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "best_practices.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
edu_efforts <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "edu_efforts.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
ext_partnerships <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "ext_partnerships.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
tools_infra <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "tools_infra.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
comm_building <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "comm_building.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
project_support <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "project_support.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
advocacy_policy <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "advocacy_policy.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
funding_support <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "funding_support.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
ospo_ops <- read_tsv(file.path(cfg$data_path, "ospo_ops.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE, skip_empty_rows = FALSE)
```

Change df entries from "yes" and "no" to numeric so we can count the yeses.

```{r}
bp2 <- best_practices |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))
```

Let's call this metric "reach", because it's about the number of people engaging with it.
```{r}
rowSums(bp2, na.rm = TRUE) > 0
reach <- sum(rowSums(bp2, na.rm = TRUE) > 0)
reach
```

Great. Let's repeat this for all nine activity categories.

```{r}
edu2 <- edu_efforts |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))

ext2 <- ext_partnerships |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))

tools2 <- tools_infra |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))

cb2 <- comm_building |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))

ps2 <- project_support |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))

ap2 <- advocacy_policy |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))

fs2 <- funding_support |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))

ospo2 <- ospo_ops |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ recode_values(.x, "Yes" ~ 1, "No" ~ 0)))
```

```{r}
df_list2 <- list(bp2, edu2, ext2, tools2, cb2, ps2, ap2, fs2, ospo2)
names(df_list2) <- c("bp", "edu", "ext", "tools", "cb", "ps", "ap", "fs", "ospo")

reach_scores <- sapply(df_list2, function(x) 
sum(rowSums(x, na.rm = TRUE) > 0)
)
reach_scores <- sort(reach_scores, decreasing = TRUE)
reach_scores
```

Print as percentages

```{r}
pcts <- round(reach_scores/nrow(df_list2[[1]])*100, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
df
```

Get average tasks per person

```{r}
summary_stats <- bind_cols(df_list2) |>
  mutate(total_activities = rowSums(across(everything()), na.rm = TRUE)) 

dim(summary_stats)

summary_stats  |>
  summarise(
    mean_activities = mean(total_activities),
    median_activities = median(total_activities),
    sd_activities = sd(total_activities)
  )
```

^ This show the number of activities per person, where the col # is the number of activities they could choose from (here 51)

# Which activities take the most time?

Let's say that every time an activity is ranked #1, it gets 3 points, when it's ranked #2, it gets 2 point, and when it's ranked #3, it gets 1 point.

I think in this case I will again not filter to one response per organization, since the survey said, "Answer for yourself, not the whole team." So we can interpret this as, how OSPO workers spend their time.

```{r}
activity_scores <- ranking |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(rank1, rank2, rank3),
    names_to = "rank",
    values_to = "activity"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    points = case_when(
      rank == "rank1" ~ 3,
      rank == "rank2" ~ 2,
      rank == "rank3" ~ 1
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(activity) |>
  summarise(total_score = sum(points), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total_score))

activity_scores
```

Note: from manual inspection I see that one person did not answer this question. That's where the NAs come from.

What percent of respondents ranked each task as their #1? I wonder if this method changes the ranking.
```{r}
table(ranking$rank1)
```

Cool, the order is the same.

Note: I manually reviewed the "other" answers and didn't see anything super compelling. I did add a couple of "lessons learned" based on answers that people wrote in and that I think should be survey options next time.
